For parking information, please visit this link: https://www.dc.umich.edu/about-the-dc/maps-floor-plans-hours/#parking

Exhibition Opening Event: 
- When: Friday, September 18, 5 pm to 6 pm
- Where: Duderstadt Center Gallery
- Open to the public
- Description: Please join us for the opening of this photo exhibition. The event will feature remarks by the organizers, the exhibition curators, one of the featured photojournalists, and a former Peace Corps volunteer who has stood in solidarity with the people of Gwangju since 1980. Light refreshments are provided. 

*Exhibition Description*
This photo exhibition features 90 curated images from the UNESCO-inscribed May 18 Archives. Documenting the May 18–27, 1980 democratization uprising in Gwangju, South Korea, the collection captures the shift from peaceful student protests to military violence and unified citizen resistance, carried out under a complete blackout as civilians and photojournalists risked their lives to photograph atrocities and smuggle film past cordons. Beyond serving as historical artifacts, these preserved visual truths offer a living blueprint for popular resilience against authoritarianism, transforming local trauma into a universal defense of human rights. Displaying these records at Michigan bridges 1980 Gwangju with our present moment, inviting viewers to engage past resistance in the ongoing effort to defend democracy today.

*Exhibition Composition*
The exhibit will be composed of a visual narrative comprised of six chronological sections and two additional special sections:

1. Protest (May 5–16, 1980): 
Following the collapse of Park Chung-hee’s military dictatorship in October, 1979, Gwangju students and citizens held peaceful rallies for campus autonomy and the end of martial law. Photos from this era show orderly marches and hopeful faces, capturing a society on the brink of change before the structural contradictions shifted toward state-led violence. 

2. Suppression (May 18–19, 1980): 
A new junta government led by Chun Doo-hwan extended martial law to the entire country on May 17. Students at Chonnam National University protested against the new junta government’s decision. State violence escalated as paratroopers, who were deployed to Gwangju, engaged student protesters. Streets became scenes of brutal beatings and kidnappings. Beyond documenting victims, the images on display in this section serve as primary historical evidence and legal proof of the military's methods and the sudden transformation of citizens into targets of control. 

3. Uprising (May 20–21, 1980): 
The movement shifted into a popular struggle. Vehicles lined up in Gwangju’s main thoroughfare, Geumnam-ro. This massive vehicle parade symbolized the people becoming active subjects of resistance. The military was given the order to use live ammunition against civilians. In reaction, the city became a space of voluntary mobilization and citizens emerged as historical political actors. 

4. Resistance (May 22–26, 1980): 
While isolated and cut off from communications, Gwangju established an autonomous system of self-governance. Photos in this section testify to the efforts made to establish a sense of order based on solidarity—sharing food and donating blood—rather than chaos. The formation of this "Daedong (Great Unity) Community" and the visual documentation thereof serve as foundations of democracy in South Korea. 

5. Massacre (May 27, 1980): 
The uprising was crushed by a dawn military operation. While the armed resistance ended, the resulting photographs of the aftermath reveal the stark reality of the massacre. These images became the catalyst for future truth-seeking movements and the pursuit of historical justice in South Korea. 

6. Mourning: 
Scenes of coffins, portraits, and silent vigils represent a collective ethical gaze. During this period, mourning was more than a display of grief; it was a communal act used to redefine the city’s identity and establish new moral standards for justice.

7. Special Section A: The Photographers
This special section highlights the domestic and international photographers who documented the uprising. This includes Korean journalists alongside US journalists Robin Moyer and Norman Thorpe, French correspondents Patrick Chauvel and François Lochon, and German cinematographer Jürgen Hinzpeter. Their images transcend simple reporting, reflecting a moral commitment to record and a historical duty to ensure remembrance. Rather than viewing these photos solely as evidence, the exhibition reinterprets them through a lens of photographic history—examining their context, distribution, and how they transformed raw records into social truth and collective memory.

8. Special Section B: The Peace Corps: Americans Who Helped Gwangju
When Gwangju was isolated under martial law in May 1980, four American Peace Corps volunteers—Tim Warnberg, David Lee Dolinger, Judi Chamberlin, and Paul Courtright—refused to leave, choosing instead to assist the wounded, aid foreign journalists, and ultimately expose the truth to the world. Those pivotal ten days reshaped their lives into lifelong commitments to human rights, inspiring decades of memoirs, academic writings, and testimonies. Through photographs, video footage, and personal records, this section traces their journey from eyewitnesses to active defenders of human dignity, inviting us to reflect on what it truly means to take a stand in the face of another’s suffering.

description: Seminar Summary - Ecological opportunity is often invoked to explain major evolutionary radiations, but how opportunities arise, are exploited, and ultimately become constrained remains less clear. Using insects as a lens, I explore these processes across scales: from how the transition from gymnosperm- to angiosperm-dominated ecosystems reorganized insect diversification, to how generalist interactions preceded specialization in Hymenoptera; how deep evolutionary history structures global bee biogeography; and how phylogeny and ecology shape insect elemental stoichiometry. Finally, I use the fossil history of ants to ask how competition, facilitation, and diversity dependence allow biodiversity itself to reshape future evolutionary opportunities. Together, these studies view ecological opportunity not as a single event, but as a dynamic process that is continually created, filtered, and reconstructed through deep time.

The rise of Chinese-linked criminal actors in Southeast Asia – including cyber scammers running fake online romance schemes for financial extortion – has disrupted traditional narratives of China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) infrastructure investment strategy. Counter to the "romantic" Silk Road imagery the BRI commonly draws on, these activities are forcing a reconfiguration of political and economic realities across the region, shifting attention toward changing practices of digital economy and governance along the BRI. This paper introduces the concept of 'variegated govotolerance' to explain why governments and citizens have (to varying degrees) come to tolerate, regional cybercriminal activity linked to Chinese actors.

Tom Narins is an associate professor of geography, planning, and sustainability at the University at Albany with research interests in the critical geopolitics of China's growing engagement with the global economy.
His current research examines the political and economic tensions associated with “Global China” in terms of both traditional and digital infrastructure, with a special focus on China’s digital expansion across the Global South. As a political and economic geographer, Tom has published on sovereignty issues relating to China's Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) as well as on official Chinese lending to BRI-participant countries after the coronavirus pandemic. His work has been published in peer-reviewed journals such as: *Geopolitics; Human Geography*; *Territory, Politics, Governance*; *The Professional Geographer*; *Asian Perspective; Area*; and *The Extractive Industries and Society*.

description:
What does it really mean to have access to healthcare? Have you ever considered what it takes to provide effective, culturally responsive care in American Indian communities?

Join Dr. Sophina Calderon and Nicholas Cushman, PharmD, MHA, BCACP, for a conversation about the barriers affecting healthcare access in American Indian communities and the role pharmacists play in addressing them, from ensuring patients have access to medication to providing the culturally responsive care they need.
 
 - - -
 
McKesson Foundation Health Equity Speaker Series

Disparities in health and healthcare have been are prevalent, particularly in underserved or minority communities, as a result of a variety of factors such as birthplace, housing, education, race, age, sexual identity and other nonmedical factors. These factors are commonly referred to as the social determinants of health (SDOH). As a result of SDOH, quality healthcare and treatment can be difficult to access for many who don’t fall into the dominant group and must confront barriers to receive treatment.

Examples of barriers to adequate healthcare treatment include poverty, lack of access to quality education or positive social activities, and unhealthy environmental factors. These factors must be addressed in order to achieve positive health outcomes and equity in access to healthcare and treatment for all. To help illuminate and educate around issues involving social determinants of health, the College of Pharmacy and the McKesson Foundation have teamed up to launch the McKesson Foundation Health Equity Speaker Series.

For the past two years the College of Pharmacy at the University of Michigan in partnership with the McKesson Foundation has hosted a speaker series based on the topic of health equity. The McKesson Foundation is dedicated to advancing health outcomes for all with the mission to removing barriers to quality healthcare across the country, especially for vulnerable and underserved communities. The College of Pharmacy also has a longstanding history of fighting to address addressing disparities in healthcare and is a leader in the fight for equitable healthcare for all individuals. This alignment in values and mission of both organizations led to the provision awarding of a grant to resulted in the College of Pharmacy being awarded a grant in 2022 to launch what we now call the McKesson Foundation Health Equity Speaker Series, with the goal of educating the UM community and inspiring those around us to find solutions that address inequities in healthcare and beyond.

About our Funder, the McKesson Foundation
The McKesson Foundation is a charitable organization dedicated to improving health outcomes for vulnerable and underserved populations. It focuses on initiatives that address healthcare disparities, promote patient-centered care, and support cancer care and survivorship. Through grants, partnerships, and employee-driven giving programs, the foundation aims to foster innovative solutions that enhance community health and well-being.

event_title: A Prior-Agnostic Test for Bayesian Updating (by Cheaheon Lim and Tomasz Strzalecki)
combined_title: A Prior-Agnostic Test for Bayesian Updating (by Cheaheon Lim and Tomasz Strzalecki): Tomasz Strzalecki, Harvard University
description: We develop a test of Bayesian updating “in the field,” where the analyst observes neither the likelihood function nor the realized signals. Our test works ex post, conditional on every realized state, and is prior-agnostic in the sense that its validity does not require the agent’s prior to be “correct.” We compare our procedure to tests based on the martingale property of beliefs, which are valid only ex ante, before the state is realized, and only if the prior is correct. Whereas martingale tests are sensitive to correlation between issues, our test is robust to such dependence. Even when issues are independent, we find that our test typically has greater power relative to the martingale-based tests. In an empirical application using individual-level belief data, we illustrate how our procedure provides a more direct test of Bayesian updating than the martingale-based alternatives.

We know that classroom physical activity breaks can help children move more, interrupt prolonged sitting, and support learning—but knowing what works is only the beginning. The harder question is: How do we help schools consistently put evidence into practice? This talk explores the journey from evidence-based intervention to sustainable classroom practice, drawing on the implementation of InPACT (Interrupting Prolonged Sitting with Activity) across Michigan schools. Dr. Hasson will examine why promising physical activity interventions often fall short during implementation and how implementation science can help close the gap between adoption and everyday use. She will highlight three complementary strategies—Replicating Effective Programs, implementation teams, and implementation facilitation—and share lessons from their application in diverse school settings. The talk will introduce a precision implementation approach: rather than assuming every school needs the same support, implementation strategies can be stepped up according to the barriers, resources, and readiness of each school. Attendees will leave with practical insights into how to move beyond simply asking, "Does it work?" to asking, “What support does this setting need to make it work—and sustain it?”

Bio: 
Dr. Rebecca Hasson is the Victor L. Katch Collegiate Professor of Kinesiology and an associate professor of Movement Science at the University of Michigan. She is a nationally recognized expert in children's health, physical activity, and health equity. She created InPACT and InPACT at Home to help children be more active through fun, short activity breaks that fit easily into the school day and family routines. For more than 15 years, Dr. Hasson has worked with schools, healthcare providers, and families to develop practical, evidence-based programs that improve children's physical, mental, and emotional well-being. Her research is supported by the National Institutes of Health and the Michigan Health Endowment Fund, with a focus on making healthy lifestyles more accessible for all children. Through InPACT, her goal is to give every child the opportunity to enjoy the lifelong benefits of regular physical activity—at school, at home, and beyond.

description: The f-elements, including lanthanides and actinides, play critical roles in energy technologies, medicine, and emerging quantum computing applications, yet remain comparatively under-explored in computational chemistry compared to main block elements. This seminar will introduce Architector, a software package released in 2023 that enables the generation of molecular structures across the periodic table, with particular capabilities for f-element coordination complexes. Examples in rare-earth extraction and medical isotope chelation will illustrate how these capabilities can accelerate computational molecular design and address challenges in f-element chemistry.

event_title: CM-AMO Seminar | Witnessing Quantum Entanglement in Solid-State Materials
combined_title: CM-AMO Seminar | Witnessing Quantum Entanglement in Solid-State Materials: Yao Wang (Emory University)
description:
The rapidly developing field of quantum materials calls for increasingly precise methods to characterize and control entanglement. While foundational progress was first achieved in quantum optics and few-body quantum simulators, extending these ideas to complex many-body states in correlated materials remains a major challenge. In this talk, I will introduce the entanglement-witness framework as a practical route for characterizing entanglement through experimentally accessible solid-state measurements. I will begin with the Bell test and discuss how its underlying logic can be generalized to entanglement witnesses in material systems. Recent examples include the detection of spin entanglement in quantum magnets using neutron scattering and spin-orbital entanglement using resonant inelastic x-ray scattering. These approaches can also be extended to nonequilibrium settings, opening opportunities to manipulate entanglement with light. In the second half of the talk, I will move beyond distinguishable local degrees of freedom and consider entanglement among indistinguishable fermions. This motivates a generalized framework for multipartite electronic entanglement based on the cumulant reduced density matrix and nonlinear spectroscopic responses. With this strategy, we can further connect transport-noise measurements in cryogenic materials to an electronic entanglement metric, enabling the certification of entanglement in the fractional Chern insulating state of twisted MoTe2.

Bio: Yao Wang is an associate professor in Emory University. He received bachelor's degree from University of Science and Technology of China in 2011 and Ph.D. degree from Stanford University in 2017. After that, he worked at Harvard University as an MPHQ postdoctoral fellow. In 2020, he started his independent career as an assistant professor at Clemson University and then the College of Science Dean's assistant professor. He moved his group to Emory University in August 2023 and obtained tenure in 2026. His research interests lie in the theoretical and computational study of quantum many-body problems and their experimental correspondence in solid-state materials and quantum science. He was the recipient of the DOE early career award, AFOSR young investigator award, and the Scialog fellow.

description:
The Premodern Colloquium presents visiting scholar Matylda Urjasz-Raczko for our first event of the 2026-2027 academic year. On Tuesday, October 6th, Matylda will give a presentation which examines the figure of Bona Sforza of Aragon (1494-1557), Queen of Poland, Grand Duchess of Lithuania, Princess of Bari, Rssano in the Kingdom of Naples, and heir to the Duchy of Mila and the Kingdom of Jerusalen. It is thought not as a gender biography. Her figure and life serve as a case study to illustrate the processes taking place in the Mediterranean world and in northern and eastern Europe in the time just before the Habsburg domination in the mid-16th century. The focus is therefore on the time and places where Bona came to rule. It serves as a lens that focuses various problems related to the formation of a new balance of power and a shape of the future Europe.

description:
If you are only seeing one workshop, please SIGN-IN and refresh the Sessions page! If still having issues, click this link. 
First-Year Relationship and Sexuality Talk (FYRST) is a required, in-person, and peer-facilitated workshop that came directly from feedback and listening sessions with current University of Michigan students. Our goal is to create an accessible, supportive space for student-driven conversations where all identities and experiences are welcomed and in which students can build skills and tools around identifying goals and values and then communicate effectively about those. Workshops will be offered at multiple locations and times throughout the fall semester, so please sign up for the workshop that works for you!! First-Year Relationship Sexuality Talk (FYRST) FAQ:
“How many workshops do I have to sign up for?”
You only need to sign up for 1 workshop. Attending 1 workshop will fulfill the requirement for the training. 
“I see that there is more than one session, does it matter which one I sign up for?”
It generally does not matter which workshop you sign up for. There will be a few that are designated for specific groups such as transfer students or for students looking for accommodations. If you do not fit these groups please try to save these workshops for those that do and you are free to choose among any of the other workshops. 
“Is this workshop required?”
This workshop is required for all transfer and first-year students at the University of Michigan.
“I’ve experienced harm around relationships or sexual experiences in the past and I am worried that attending this workshop may be harmful for me.” 
Our team is aware that students who are coming into the university that have experienced harm in the past. Our workshop is specifically designed to respect and validate the experiences of survivors and has been carefully constructed to avoid any specific descriptions of violence and focus instead on themes of empowerment, communication, and boundary setting. However, if you still have concerns about programming and would like to request alternative programming, please feel free to reach out at SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.
“What if I struggle to learn in a presentation setting? I’m an active learner.”
Our workshop is built to meet a variety of learning styles, including time for self-reflection, small group sharing, and resources to take with you to work through on your own time! This workshop is meant to be interactive and inclusive. 
“Can I request accommodations?”
We considered accessibility in creating this workshop and selecting the locations in which the workshops are help. However, we recognize many places at the University are inaccessible and we've set an * next to workshops that are on the first floor and lack stairs. These workshops also will have a presentation (other workshops we do not) and are a good fit for those who might need a large font. Please sign up for those if you feel that accommodations would assist you and reach out to SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu if you are concerned or have questions. 
“I missed my workshop, what should I do ?”
Our team tracks attendance at each workshop by having participants swipe in with their MCard. If you are not able to attend the workshop you signed up for, our team will continue to send reminder emails until you have completed a workshop. In this case, please sign up for another workshop as soon as you can as the workshop is required and may fill up especially near the end of the semester. No need to contact SAPAC unless you are not able to reschedule. 
“I have had gender-based violence training before, can I get this requirement waived?”
As this workshop was designed with University of Michigan student feedback in mind, our workshop is unique to the UM community. Our curriculum focuses on individualized reflection and because of its interactive nature, each workshop will be unique to the people attending. Although we are excited you already have familiarity with the subject, this workshop is required for every first year and transfer student. 
“I’m a commuter/non-traditional student, do I still have to attend?"
Yes, this workshop is required for every first-year and transfer student - not only do we want every student to benefit from having this time to connect with peers, but we also want to make sure your peers benefit from what you bring to our community. If you have any concerns or questions about being able to participate, please contact SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.
“I still have questions! Who should I contact?"
Please contact us at SAPAC-FYRST@umich.edu.
